title: The problem: quality, not just access
plain_summary: Tanzania has cut maternal and child deaths, but the care mothers and children actually receive at local clinics varies widely. Poor quality, not just poor access, is what keeps deaths high.

title: What the study measured
plain_summary: Using Tanzania's Star Rating Assessment, trained teams scored 2,583 primary health facilities across 10 regions (2021–2022) on 12 maternal & child health indicators. A facility had to score at least 80% to 'meet' the quality standard.

title: How facilities scored
plain_summary: Only about 1 in 10 facilities met the overall standard. Maternal death reviews were the bright spot (79.6%), but most of the 12 indicators were met by fewer than half of facilities.

title: The biggest gaps
plain_summary: The three weakest areas were cervical cancer screening (7.7%), emergency obstetric medicines and supplies (16.4%), and postnatal & newborn care with dedicated neonatal/KMC space (15.2% of hospitals and health centres).

title: What predicts better quality
plain_summary: Higher-level facilities, public ownership, enough nurses, and functional management and quality-improvement teams all strongly predicted meeting the standard. Urban vs rural made no significant difference.

title: What it means and what to fix
plain_summary: The study points to concrete fixes: train and mentor providers, make quality-improvement and management teams functional, stock emergency supplies, build newborn care spaces, and expand cervical screening.
